 ED flags donations to Jauhar university in attachment order against Azam Khan
 The Mohammad Ali Jauhar University Trust, founded and controlled by Khan, received donations from “non-genuine sources”, including under the “political influence” of SP patriarch Mulayam Singh Yadav , the Enforcement Directorate said
 Published on: Oct 30, 2026, 07:41:00 IST By Neeraj Chauhan , New Delhi Prefer HT on Google Share via 
 Copy link 
 The Mohammad Ali Jauhar University Trust, founded and controlled by Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Azam Khan, received donations from “non-genuine sources”, including under the “political influence” of SP patriarch Mulayam Singh Yadav , the Enforcement Directorate said in a provisional order issued on Wednesday for attaching land properties of the university. HT has seen a copy of the order.
 India News ED said in the order that in an October 5 statement to the agency, Om Prakash Agarwal, general secretary of the Meerut-based City Educational and Social Welfare Society and KSD Charitable Trust, said that he donated ₹ 5.23 crore and ₹ 1 crore, through these two entities , to the trust for funding construction.
 It added that Agarwal claimed these contributions were made under the influence of Mulayam Singh Yadav at a gathering in Delhi in 2012, in the presence of Azam Khan. He added that his (Agarwal’s) wife, Sarojini Agarwal, then a member of the legislative council in Uttar Pradesh, recommended construction work at the university from her MLC fund on directions conveyed by SRS Yadav on behalf of Mulayam Singh Yadav. Mulayam Singh Yadav died in October 2022 after a prolonged illness.
 SP spokesperson Udaiveer Singh said, “ED, CBI, Income Tax department are all (Prime Minister) Narendra Modi and the BJP’s frontal organisations. They act according to the convenience of the BJP. Azam Khan has been harassed since Modi’s party came to power in UP. He made this university for providing education to the poor families in Rampur and nearby areas. We all know ED’s proceedings are biased.”
 State BJP chief spokesperson Dinesh Pratap Singh said the SP has habit of branding every investigation as political vendetta when its leaders face law. “ED, CBI, I-T are independent agencies working as per law and court monitoring. If the SP believes Azam Khan built a university for the poor, why are there charges of land grabbing from farmers, fake documents and money laundering? The question is not education, but loot in name of education,” Singh said.
 “When agencies act against corruption, the SP cries conspiracy. Courts have not given clean chit to Azam Khan, they have convicted him in several cases. Instead of defending land grab, the SP should answer people of Rampur,” he added.
 ED’s provisional attachment order, dated October 28 , and issued under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) was used to attach attaching land and buildings belonging to Jauhar university worth ₹ 1,170 crore at current market prices .
 ED further claimed in its order that during his questioning by ED on October 13 inside Rampur District Jail, Khan acknowledged that Agarwal may have made a donation on the advice of Mulayam Singh Yadav. He told ED -- his statement is part of the attachment order -- that the donations were made for a noble cause, for which he was grateful.
 HT tried to reach out to Khan’s lawyers but did not get a response.
 Subsequently, according to the ED order, another unexplained donation of ₹ 5.6 crore was received from an individual, who failed to appear before the agency. Another company, A&S Enterprises, also gave donations worth ₹ 40 lakh to the trust against which it received government contracts worth ₹ 25 crore, the order alleged, without specifying the details of the government orders.
 Stressing that these donations totalling ₹ 12.29 crore were received from “non-genuine sources”, the ED order said a substantial amount “was not voluntary charitable giving and cannot therefore be accepted as a legitimate source of the capital expenditure”.
 ED has claimed in its attachment order that about five hectares of government river land was enclosed within a boundary wall of the university without any proposal or lawful authority. And citing the enquiry report of the district magistrate of Rampur, ED has alleged in its orderthat 45 plots at Singankheda village that are “enemy property held by a resident of Pakistan” were leaded to the trust in 2007, and the lease cancelled just a month later at the request of the District Magistrate, although the land remained in the possession of the university.
 ED has claimed that the sub-registrar office at Rampur, on October 16, submitted certified copies of 115 sale deeds that were executed in favour of the Trust; the land on which the university stands was acquired for a total consideration of ₹ 4.63 crore. “The total cost of the campus, comprising the land and the construction, therefore amounts to ₹ 499.09 crore ( ₹ 494.46 crore and ₹ 4.63 crore). This figure covers only the land acquired through registered sale deeds. It does not include the enemy property, government river land and public-use land which, as found in the inquiry of the DM and as stated by the former Tehsildar, came under the control of the university without any lawful acquisition or through exchange orders held to be irregular,” ED said in its statement. 
 In his statement to ED, Azam Khan said he “did not recall how the land of the university was acquired and had no information on how much was purchased, taken from the government or received as a gift, and that these details are held by the university office”.
 ED has concluded in its order that the university was established and expanded through diversion of government contract funds and construction material, execution of government works on its private campus, receipt of non-genuine donations, and extortion. The agency’s order further alleges that contacts worth ₹ 23.43 crore, including a pandal, an OBC hostel, and a hospital block , were executed at the private university by UP Jal Nigam. Khan was the chairman of the Jal Nigam at the time.
 “A public asset created with state funds was thereby converted into the private property of the university by successive alteration of the sanction conditions, which Azam Khan was unable to explain,” ED said in its order.
 ABOUT THE AUTHOR Neeraj Chauhan Neeraj Chauhan is a senior journalist with Hindustan Times and an investigative reporter specialising in national security, terrorism, organised crime, narcotics, corruption, financial crime and complex investigations. With over 21 years of experience across Hindustan Times, The Times of India, The Indian Express and The Pioneer, he has built deep expertise in India’s internal security and law-enforcement landscape. Neeraj has extensively covered India’s principal investigative, intelligence and security agencies, including the NIA, CBI, ED, IB, R&AW, MHA and other central security forces. His work has included deeply reported investigations into terrorism, terror financing, cross-border crime, narcotics trafficking, cybercrime, financial fraud and political and corporate corruption. He has reported on some of the most significant terror attacks and security developments in India over the past two decades, including the Delhi serial blasts, the 26/11 Mumbai attacks, the 2019 Pulwama terror attack and the recent Pahalgam attack. His reporting has also chronicled the rise and decline of the Indian Mujahideen, the activities and subsequent crackdown on the Popular Front of India (PFI), Islamist extremist networks, the conflict in Jammu and Kashmir, insurgencies in the Northeast and Maoist violence. Some of Neeraj’s major breaking stories are in Aryan Khan drug case, Sushant Singh Rajput suicide, interception of a 3,000-kg Afghan heroin consignment worth about ₹21,000 crore at Mundra port, Sri Lanka easter bombings, Aarushi-Hemraj murders in Noida, 2G scam, coal block allocation scam, AgustWestland VVIP chopper deal and major bank frauds and extradition cases involving Mehul Choksi, Nirav Modi and Vijay Mallya. His reporting is marked by an ability to cultivate sources, analyse confidential and complex documents, and follow investigations over several years—from the initial breakthrough to chargesheets, trials and international legal proceedings. He specialises in making complicated security and investigative developments accessible while examining their wider implications for governance and public policy. A Chevening South Asia Journalism Programme Fellow at the University of Westminster, Neeraj also spent time at the Financial Times as part of the fellowship. He was also a Robert Bosch Media Ambassadors India-Germany Fellow, studying at the University of Tübingen and working with Der Tagesspiegel in Berlin. He has previously taught investigative journalism and crime reporting as a guest faculty member at the Times School of Journalism. Over more than two decades, Neeraj has established himself as an authoritative voice on India’s national security and investigative landscape, with his reporting closely followed by officials, investigators, lawyers, policymakers and readers seeking insight into some of the country’s most complex and consequential developments.
